frase_gancho.texto: The old man who carried fire on his head.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the fire that renews, we move on to another god of renewal, the god of the earth. Look for a clay sculpture in a skin costume whose open mouth reveals a priest’s face.

guion_corto.texto: This old man of volcanic stone, seated with his legs crossed and his body hunched, is Huehuetéotl, the Old God of Fire. Notice his wrinkled face, his large round ear ornaments, and the vessel on his head, carved with rhombuses and crosses, where embers and copal were burned. He is the same god you saw in clay in the previous hall, but here he is a stone sculpture, much larger. The Teotihuacán people inherited him from Cuicuilco, the city buried by the volcano. For them, fire was the center of the home and of the world: what gives warmth, and also what destroys. A grandfather with a hearth on his head.

guion_largo.texto:
The Old God of Fire has a very long history. The oldest images of this old man with a brazier appear in the Highlands more than two thousand years ago, in Cuicuilco, the city that ended up covered by lava from the Xitle volcano. That his cult survived and became even more important in Teotihuacán suggests that those who lived beside volcanoes understood him better than anyone: fire gave life and could take it away.

Look at him slowly. He is seated, with his hands on his knees, his joints bent and his torso sunken under the weight. Wrinkles surround his eyes and mouth, and that toothless mouth speaks of the many years of its owner. On top of his head he carries the vessel of fire, with edges decorated with rhombuses and crosses. It is a body of simple lines, and yet very expressive.

That vessel was not an ornament. In it, copal, wood and embers were burned, and the smoke rose to the sky like a message for the gods. Images of this god have been found in different parts of the city, and that suggests his cult did not belong only to the State, but also to families. Fire lived at the center of the house, and for that reason the Old God was, in a way, the grandfather of every home.

A thousand years later, the Mexica called him Huehuetéotl or Xiuhtecuhtli, and placed him at the center of the universe. You already know how they honored him every fifty-two years, with the New Fire. In the Mexica Hall you will find him again, and you will see that the features of this old man of stone traveled more than a thousand years almost without changing: the brazier, the wrinkles, the hunched posture.

There is an irony in the history of this city. Around the year 550 of our era, a fire devastated buildings in the ceremonial center, especially along the Avenue of the Dead: temples were burned and sculptures were broken. We do not know whether it was an invasion, an internal rebellion, or both. Afterward, Teotihuacán lost its power and, within a few generations, was left almost empty. Fire, which they had so deeply respected, brought the city to an end.

Notice the gesture. The old man does not hold the fire in his hands: he carries it on his head, the way heavy loads are carried. It is an image of effort and patience, that of someone who keeps the household flame burning throughout an entire life. Some are reminded of a grandfather; others, of a bearer of the world.

The stone it was made from is hard and rough, and working it without metal tools was slow. Every wrinkle you see took time. In a city that preferred idealized, ageless faces, like the masks that come next, this wrinkled old man is an exception, and that is why he seems so human. He is the grandfather of fire, not a distant god.

So, between Cuicuilco and the city of the Mexica, there is an old man who spans more than one thousand five hundred years of history. If you are looking for a thread that ties together the halls you have walked through, this is one of the firmest: fire as memory, as danger and as home.

texto: Count the wrinkles around his eyes and his mouth
Notice the hands on the knees and the hunched body
Look for the rhombuses and crosses carved on the vessel of fire

texto.Material: Carved volcanic stone (andesite/trachyte) with traces of stucco and pigment
texto.Dimensions: 65 cm high x 63 cm wide x 66 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: This fire god only existed to inspire fear.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Huehuetéotl was a close, familiar god: the grandfather of the home, the fire of the kitchen and of the temple.
